overview: This file documents Tokyo Imperial University's gift of a large collection of Japanese archaeological specimens to Harvard University for Harvard's 1936 tercentenary. It contains a State Department cross-reference, two closely related copies of Embassy despatch No. 1929, a January 1936 letter requesting American assistance with customs inspection, packing and addressing information for four cases, and an extensive catalogue of pottery, stone, bone, shell, and clay artifacts with Japanese provenances. Together the documents trace the gift's diplomatic, institutional, logistical, and scholarly dimensions, including shipment aboard the Hokkai Maru from Yokohama to Boston via Los Angeles, Panama, and New York.

people.name: Joseph C. Grew
people.role: U.S. Ambassador to Japan; identified on the file note as the reporting officer

people.name: Munshion Daville
people.role: Unidentified Tokyo addressee, probably an American diplomatic official; the name is badly corrupted in the OCR

subfiles.title: File note cross-referencing the Harvard tercentenary gift
subfiles.about: The filing note directs researchers to another decimal-file location for despatch No. 1929 concerning Tokyo Imperial University's archaeological gift to Harvard.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references 093.941-Harvard University/1 for despatch No. 1929 from Japan, attributed to Grew and dated July 3, 1936. It identifies the subject as Tokyo Imperial University's presentation of Japanese archaeological specimens for Harvard's tercentenary.

subfiles.title: Incomplete duplicate copy of despatch No. 1929
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy in Japan
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports the proposed archaeological gift and its shipment to Boston aboard the Hokkai Maru.
subfiles.summary: This incomplete or duplicate copy reports that Tokyo Imperial University will give Harvard University four boxes of Japanese archaeological specimens for the tercentenary. It says the Hokkai Maru is scheduled to reach Boston on August 13, but the surviving text ends in mid-sentence.

subfiles.title: Dated copy of despatch No. 1929
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy formally notifies the State Department of Tokyo Imperial University's gift to Harvard and its planned shipment.
subfiles.summary: The dated Tokyo copy repeats the report that four wooden boxes of archaeological specimens are being presented to Harvard University. It gives an August 15 arrival date for the Hokkai Maru, differing from the August 13 date on pages 2 and 4. This copy also ends in mid-sentence.

subfiles.title: Eguchi letter requesting customs assistance
subfiles.from: S. Eguchi, Secretary, Tokyo Imperial University
subfiles.to: Munshion Daville, unidentified American official in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Eguchi asks for help securing favorable customs examination of the four cases of archaeological material destined for Harvard.
subfiles.summary: Writing from the president's office, Eguchi explains that the university has selected and packed an archaeological collection to commemorate Harvard's forthcoming tercentenary. He requests assistance from the recipient's government with customs inspection so that the material will reach its destination safely. The letter names the Osaka Shosen Kaisha freighter Hokkai Maru and gives its projected route from Yokohama through Los Angeles, Panama, and New York to Boston.

subfiles.title: Packing dimensions and shipping addresses for four cases
subfiles.to: Probable museum director at Harvard University
subfiles.about: The sheet records the dimensions and weights of four cases and supplies their destination and return-address markings.
subfiles.summary: The page tabulates measurements and weights for four wooden boxes, although several figures are obscured by OCR errors. It then gives a shipping label addressed to a Harvard director in Cambridge and a badly corrupted return label for Tokyo Imperial University. The recipient was probably Donald Scott, then associated with the direction of Harvard's anthropological museum, but the OCR name is highly uncertain.

subfiles.title: Catalogue of Japanese archaeological specimens
subfiles.about: The enclosure catalogues the pottery, stone, bone, shell, and clay artifacts included in the university's gift.
subfiles.summary: Following an enclosure heading, the surviving catalogue pages list numbered artifacts and their localities, extending through specimen No. 250 with gaps and grouped number ranges. The collection includes Moroiso-, Atsude-shiki-, Usude-shiki-, Entō-, and Kamegaoka-type pottery; chipped and polished stone tools; arrowheads, drills, sinkers, scrapers, bone points, shell ornaments, and fragments of clay human figures. Provenances span the Kantō, central Japanese, and northeastern Japanese districts and historical provinces including Sagami, Hitachi, Musashi, Kai, Shinano, Mutsu, Iwaki, and Shimōsa. Numerous object and place names are distorted in the OCR, and the first catalogue page appears to be absent or illegible because page 7 begins with the internal page number “-2-.”

subfiles.title: End separator sheet
subfiles.about: A nearly blank sheet marks the end of the file or filming unit.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the word “LITTLE” and a long broken rule. It carries no substantive correspondence or archaeological information and appears to be a separator or filming artifact.

interest: The file is especially useful for connecting cultural diplomacy with the practical formation of an American museum collection: it preserves not only the official announcement but also customs concerns, shipping arrangements, case specifications, and artifact-level provenance. The long inventory offers evidence about Japanese archaeological classification and regional collecting practices in the 1930s, including early use of pottery types such as Moroiso and Kamegaoka. The duplicated despatch copies, with conflicting Boston arrival dates, and the severely corrupted names and localities also illustrate the evidentiary problems posed by carbon copies, incomplete archival survival, and OCR of historical records.
